author: carlosgraffi
body:
Two coordination documents for **Actions & Plans v2 (MEED)**, deliberately kept out of [#2956](https://github.com/Open-Earth-Foundation/CityCatalyst/pull/2956) so they can be read now rather than after a 109-file review.

Docs only — no code, no behaviour change.

### `MeedReferenceDataContractDiff.md`

The field-by-field analysis of the hiap-meed reference-data contract against what the module actually renders, plus its resolution.

It was written against the first draft of [#2982](https://github.com/Open-Earth-Foundation/CityCatalyst/pull/2982), which dropped 17 fields the UI depends on. **6 of the 7 asks were then delivered in full**; the seventh (the 5-item caps) was declined with sound reasoning. Each ask now carries its outcome inline, so the document is both the record of what was asked and the current state.

Two things worth flagging to reviewers:

- **A correction on our side.** The earlier version credited the migration with uncapped policy evidence. That was wrong — the upstream default is already 5 per action and hiap-meed doesn't pass `top_evidence_limit`. Corrected here. @Mirco, this was in the doc you worked from.
- **The `sector` ask was wrong, and it exposed a bug of ours.** Global API provides no top-level action sector — verified across all 102 catalog actions. Deriving it from `emissions.sector_number` is our work. That check also showed `actionCatalog.ts:63` reads a `sector` key that has never existed, so **every action currently displays "Cross-sector"** in the ranked table, top-pick cards and detail panel.

**Three small asks remain open, all non-blocking:** structured `warnings` (the current English prose can't be translated, and the module ships in 5 languages), `datasource`/`version_label` on city indicators, and a documented vocabulary for `policy_support_category`.

An earlier revision of this PR raised a fourth — an eighth reference-data endpoint for legal assessments, so the Regulations screen could render at step 3 instead of after the ranking. **That has been retracted.** The prototype solves it with no new endpoint: `RegulationsLaws.tsx` calls the prioritizer on mount when nothing is cached (`createExplanations: false`, so no LLM) and renders the legal screening from the response. It works because hard filters evaluate city, country and the action catalog only — they are preference-independent, so running before steps 4–6 are answered gives the same verdicts. It's a frontend fix, and the doc now says so.

On screen coverage, the doc also corrects a metric I'd been quoting. "6 of 11 screens render live data" conflated an input form, a summary and a transition screen with genuine gaps. **Only two screens are unfinished:** results, which legitimately needs a ranking, and regulations — the one real defect, per the ask above.

The remaining work splits into two piles that **do not block each other**:

**Deploy plumbing — reviewable now, independent of the module.** Two values are missing from the deploy workflows: `HIAP_MEED_API_URL` and `MEED_MODULE` in dev's `NEXT_PUBLIC_FEATURE_FLAGS`. Plain repo edits, no secrets, no cluster operations. The doc pins the exact value per environment, verified from `hiap-meed/k8s/service-{dev,test,prod}.yml`, so this is a review rather than an investigation.

Worth stating plainly: **these are inert until our code lands.** On `develop` today the MEED module has zero files and `MEED_MODULE` isn't even a defined flag — so the flag string does nothing and the env var is unused. They can go in whenever it suits, with no ordering dependency in either direction.

**Module delivery — our sequencing choice.** #2956 is held in draft **deliberately**, so that what reaches dev does something real rather than a flag-gated shell. That's a product decision, not a blocker awaiting review.

**One open decision for whoever owns the deploy pipeline**, set out at the end of the doc. `hiap-meed-service-dev` is `ClusterIP` with no ingress, so `HIAP_MEED_API_URL` can only be exercised from inside the cluster — the first genuine test of the connection has to happen on dev, after something is merged.

Worth knowing: **#2956 is not all-or-nothing.** It's 14 commits along deliberate seams and several stand alone — including `803b5da6a`, a root-level theme fix (`radii.full` as a stadium radius) that is a defect on `develop` today and unrelated to MEED entirely. Registration, contract types and a connectivity-only change can each land ahead of any screen. The doc lists which commits are independently mergeable and takes no position on how to slice them.

The doc also lists 11 frontend defects we own and will fix, four of which are visible today (the "Cross-sector" bug above; project costs rendering 1000× too high because `amount_unit` is `CLP_thousands` and we assume millions; 15% of actions showing "Unknown route"; and Chilean cities described with the wrong profile).

One note for whoever picks up the integration: **prioritize does not depend on #2982.** The hiap-meed pod fetches its own reference data, so the ranking can be wired while the GETs are still in review.

### Note

`MeedModuleImplementation.md` is referenced but not included — it lands with #2956, so that link resolves once that PR merges.

author: davdhacs
body:
## Description

Scanner V4 Indexer and Matcher listen on `0.0.0.0` (IPv4 only), making them unreachable on IPv6-only clusters where Kubernetes routes traffic via IPv6 pod IPs. This cascades into image enrichment failures, missing vulnerability data, and empty policy violations on IPv6-only and dual-stack IPv6-primary clusters.

Additionally, several other components use hardcoded `127.0.0.1` addresses, have IPv6-broken port detection heuristics, or use an incomplete IPv6 regex for policy evaluation.

**Changes (12 files):**

| Component | Issue | Fix |
|-----------|-------|-----|
| Scanner V4 Helm configs | `0.0.0.0:8443` (IPv4 only) | `:8443` (dual-stack) |
| Scanner V4 Go defaults | `127.0.0.1:8443` | `localhost:8443` |
| Central DB health check | `pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1` | `-h localhost` |
| Scanner V4 DB health check | same | same |
| Node scanning endpoint | `127.0.0.1:8444` default | `localhost:8444` |
| Sensor pprof server | `127.0.0.1:6060` | `localhost:6060` |
| Debug handler | `127.0.0.1:<port>` | `localhost:<port>` |
| Cluster validation | `strings.Contains(":") ` port check | `net.SplitHostPort` |
| TLS credential expiry | colon-based port detection | `net.SplitHostPort` |
| Helm port heuristic | assumes colon means port | handles `[host]:port` bracket notation |
| Boolean policy engine | IPv6 regex misses `::1`, `fe80::`, `::` | rewritten to match all valid forms |

Found via IPv6-only KinD e2e testing (PR #22234). The Scanner V4 listen address is the critical fix that unblocks image scanning on IPv6 clusters.

- [ ] [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/stackrox/stackrox/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md) is updated **OR** update is not needed
- [x] [documentation PR](https://spaces.redhat.com/display/StackRox/Submitting+a+User+Documentation+Pull+Request) is created and is linked above **OR** is not needed

## Testing and quality

- [x] the change is production ready: the change is [GA](https://github.com/stackrox/stackrox/blob/master/PR_GA.md), or otherwise the functionality is gated by a [feature flag](https://github.com/stackrox/stackrox/blob/master/pkg/features/README.md)
- [ ] CI results are [inspected](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1d5ga073jkv4CO1kAJqp8MPGpC6E1bwyrCGZ7S5wKg3w/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.w4ercgtcg0xp)

### Automated testing

- [x] modified existing tests

### How I validated my change

These issues were discovered by running the full QA e2e test suite on IPv6-only KinD clusters (PR #22234). The Scanner V4 `0.0.0.0` listen address was independently identified by two code investigation agents as the root cause for image enrichment, enforcement, and vulnerability scan failures on IPv6.

author: rjwalters
body:
## Summary

Documents a first attempt at issue #235 (DR-024's lever 2: re-ratio
`por_output_chain`'s shared-`IBIAS` consumer mirror diode `XMBD` so the
cell's delivered current clears its 0.44x / 220 nA floor) and why it is
**not** landed by this PR.

## What was tried (not committed)

Scaling `XMBD` and every device in `por_output_chain` whose current is a
fixed ratio against `XMBD`'s own gate voltage (`XMN1`, `XMPD`, `XMP2`,
`XMND`, `XMDGPT`, `XMDGNT`, `XMPT`, `XMDANT`, `XMDBPT`) by a uniform 10x in
width, preserving every ratio in `design/por_output_chain.md`'s "Device
sizing" table exactly.

- **The targeted metric improved as intended**: re-running
  `sim/por-output-chain-ibias-sharing/` against the resized netlist moved
  the released-state worst corner (`ss_-40c_2.97v`) from 91.03 nA (0.182x)
  to 247.81 nA (0.496x) — clearing the 220 nA floor with ~13% margin.
- **But `sim/por-output-chain-deglitch/` regressed in a new, larger way**:
  most PVT points fail to resolve `RESETn`'s post-dip re-assertion
  measurement at all (`out of interval`), because `RESETn` is already
  re-asserting itself spontaneously, well before the qualifying brownout
  dip, at the idealised *nominal* `IBIAS` DUT. Tracing one corner shows this
  is the same release-edge relaxation-loop mechanism `DR-016` diagnosed and
  fixed for issue #56 — reopened because the resize changes the trip
  detector's node-voltage operating point even though it preserves current
  ratios.

Landing that resize would violate CLAUDE.md's "no claim without a
testbench": it regresses the cell's own release behavior on the majority of
the PVT grid, a bigger problem than the floor shortfall it targets. So no
netlist, layout, or testbench file is changed by this PR — the working tree
that produced the numbers above is discarded, not committed.

## Changes

- Adds `spec/decision-records/DR-026-por-output-chain-xmbd-reratio-attempt-startup-regression.md`,
  documenting the attempt, the diagnosis (tracing the regression back to
  DR-016's relaxation-loop mechanism), and what the next attempt needs:
  re-derive the trip detector (`XMDAPI`/`XMDANT`, `XMDBNI`/`XMDBPT`,
  `XMRLK`) as a system against the new node voltage rather than assuming
  ratio-preservation is sufficient, and/or try a smaller widening factor
  before committing to a full trip-detector re-derivation.

No other files change.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] Diagnostic evidence for the attempted resize is recorded (this PR).
- [ ] Issue #235's actual acceptance checklist (working re-ratio, three-testbench
      re-run, comparator/IQ re-checks, DRC/LVS, decision record recording the
      *adopted* ratios) remains open — this PR does not close it.

## Test Plan

- N/A for this PR's own diff (documentation only, no `design/`, `sim/`,
  or `layout/` file changes).
- The exploratory runs cited in DR-026 were `--no-write` debug runs against
  a working tree that is not part of this PR; they are cited as evidence in
  the decision record's prose, not as `sim/` records, per the harness
  convention that only committed runs mint record IDs.

## Follow-up

Issue #235 is being moved to `loom:blocked` (not closed) with a comment
pointing at this PR and DR-026, so the next attempt can start from the
diagnosis here instead of repeating the 10x-scale attempt.

author: felixkwasisarpong
body:
## Why
The feed is where users actually spend time — so surface the platform's career intelligence *there*, interleaved between jobs (the pattern in the "Do you have these skills?" card), chosen by what helps this user most. Turns a passive job list into an active, self-tailoring surface.

## Cards (v1 — all corpus-grounded, honest, extensible)
- **pivot** — best adjacent field with more openings / a visa edge (`suggestPivotTarget`)
- **skill_boost** — real in-demand skills of the user's field their résumé doesn't surface; **tapping one affirms it and re-scores the feed** (the interactive "do you have these skills?" pattern)
- **sharpen** — a split résumé signal costs matches in both lanes → pick one

Nothing is invented — every number/skill comes from the live corpus + the résumé's real overlap. Returns nothing when there's no useful, grounded thing to say.

## Architecture (add a new card type in one place)
- `lib/feed/insights.ts` — `buildFeedInsights(resume, profiles)` → prioritized cards (4 tests).
- `/api/feed/insights` — per-user cards.
- `/api/resume/skills/affirm` — appends affirmed skills to `top_skills` + bumps `updated_at` → batch scorer re-scores.
- `components/feed/{useFeedInsights,FeedInsightCard}` — fetch + persisted per-card dismissal (keyed by advice, so a card returns only when the advice changes) + card UI.

The big Tier-1 item: functions become values, unlocking higher-order programming.

## First-class functions
- New `VAL_FUNC` value type wrapping a function definition. A bare function name now evaluates to a function value, so you can store it, pass it, and call it:

- `savomap(@a, fn)`, `savofilter(@a, fn)`, `savoreduce(@a, fn, init)`, and `savosort(@a [, cmp])` (default order for numbers/strings, or a custom comparator). Composition works: `savomap(savofilter(xs, isEven), double)`.

## What this does

Removes nested `.gitignore` lines under `sdk/` that restate rules an ancestor
`.gitignore` already provides, and deletes the files that turned out to be redundant in
their entirety.

**Why the removed lines are provably no-ops.** Git applies **every** `.gitignore` from the
work tree root down to the file being checked; the rules are cumulative, and on conflict the
deepest file wins. None of the 114 rules in the root `.gitignore` is anchored with a leading
`/`, so every root rule already applies at every depth in the tree. A nested rule that
repeats an ancestor rule therefore cannot change which files are ignored. It is dead weight:
it does nothing today, and it silently goes stale whenever the ancestor changes.

Every line removed here appears verbatim in an ancestor `.gitignore`. Only exact,
whitespace-trimmed string equality was treated as a duplicate. Nothing was removed on a
fuzzy or prefix match, since `.vscode` and `.vs/` are different rules, as are `bin` and
`bin/`.

## Changes

### Files deleted (redundant in their entirety)

| File | Why it is fully redundant |
| --- | --- |
| `sdk/modelsrepository/Azure.IoT.ModelsRepository/.gitignore` | Its entire contents were one line, `launchSettings.json` (root line 12). |
| `sdk/digitaltwins/Azure.DigitalTwins.Core/.gitignore` | All four rules come from an ancestor. `launchSettings.json` is root line 12, and `*.config.json` plus both of its negations (`!*common.config.json`, `!*common.test.assets.config.json`) already appear in `sdk/digitaltwins/.gitignore` **in the same relative order**. |

### Files trimmed

The three genuinely local entries are kept: `stress-test-resources.json`, `charts`, `.vscode`. |
| `sdk/contentunderstanding/.gitignore` | `*.bicep.env` (root line 138) |
| `sdk/keyvault/.gitignore` | `*.pfx` (root line 135) |
| `sdk/openai/.gitignore` | `TempTypeSpecFiles/` (root line 183) |

16 deletions, 0 additions. Comments, blank-line grouping, ordering, and line endings of every
surviving rule are preserved.

## Deliberately left alone

**Any `.gitignore` inside a `samples/` directory**, including
`sdk/cloudmachine/Azure.Projects/samples/**`,

everything under the repository-root `samples/` tree. These are by far the largest offenders,
carrying 58, 56, 56, 7, 4, 4 and 2 duplicate rules respectively, and they are left completely
untouched on purpose: standalone samples are exported and downloaded **outside** the
repository, where the root `.gitignore` does not exist. A complete, self-contained
`.gitignore` is very likely correct there.

**`eng/common`.** `eng/common/.gitignore` restates `node_modules/` from root line 170, but
that directory is synced from `Azure/azure-sdk-tools` into every language repo, so a change
here would be reverted by the next sync and has to be made upstream instead. Left untouched.

**Rules that are only correct because they are scoped.** Nested rules were *not* hoisted up
into the root, because their locality is load-bearing. Several would match committed files

The remaining nested files under `sdk/` contain zero duplicated rules and are untouched.

A freshly pulled tree contains no build artifacts, so the raw output was empty on both sides

body:
## Problem (follow-up to #22)

On-device testing on the Pixel 9 Pro after #22 gave a **split result**:

| Repro | Result |
|---|---|
| **#1 — ladder Axis-B bitrate step** | ✅ Fixed & device-verified (in-place `RtpSender` bitrate; real R0→R1 step, no crash). |
| **#2 — renegotiation during reconnect** | ❌ **Still crashed** — same native `SIGABRT` (`network_thread`, `libc++ … disengaged value`, WebRTC 144). |

**Captured trigger:** a **back-to-back reconnect** — a reconnect resumed (`Reconnecting→Live`), then a Wi-Fi handover fired *another* reconnect **~1 s later**, tearing down the just-built PeerConnection mid-setup. That native teardown/setup race is **below** #22's Kotlin `transportMutex` (`room.disconnect()`'s native teardown outlives the `suspend`). And we're **already on the latest** livekit-android 2.27.0 / WebRTC 144.7559.09 — nothing to bump to — so the only lever we own is **reducing reconnect churn**.

## Fix — post-recovery quiet period

- `ReconnectionController` tracks `lastRecoveredMs`, stamped on **every** successful connect (the initial `Connected` **and** every reconnect/resume).
- A **proactive** reconnect (network-handover / media-stall) within `RECOVERY_QUIET_MS` (5 s) of that is **suppressed**, so the just-built native PeerConnection drains before any new `connect()`+`publish()`.
- **Genuine `Disconnected`/`Failed` drops are never gated** (a real death must recover now); the `NONE` proactive-`Reconnecting` is state-only and untouched.

## Verification

- ✅ **On-device (Pixel 9 Pro):** the exact sequence that killed the process before (airplane full-drops + Wi-Fi handovers) now **survives** — PID stable, **zero crash signatures**, and the gate visibly logs `transport handover within post-recovery quiet period — skipping` for the ~1 s-after-resume handover, while normal handovers (>5 s later) and genuine drops still reconnect.
- ✅ `./gradlew :app:testDebugUnitTest` → **80 pass** (+4 quiet-period cases: suppress in-window, fire after window, genuine-drop-not-gated, initial-connect-in-window).
- ✅ `:app:assembleDebug` clean.
- ✅ Fresh-context adversarial review → **SHIP** (its one real finding — the initial-connect window — is fixed in this PR by stamping on the initial `Connected`).

## Honesty / limits

- This is a **churn-reduction mitigation, not a cure.** The disengaged-optional bug is in WebRTC 144 (libc++ hardening → hard abort); a *single* renegotiation on a truly marginal link could still trip it. The real fix is upstream — deferred because we're already on the newest SDK.
- RESILIENCE.md Appendix B + §1 matrix updated to this honest split result.
- Next lever if ever needed: a brief post-teardown settle delay in `connect()` (documented, not added — the on-device re-run showed the quiet period alone stops the reproduced crash).

author: baileyrd
body:
Closes #270.

## The bug

Three background loops (the folder watcher, the reminder scheduler, the promotion-backlog nudge) could all silently stop working — a panic, a bug, anything that ends the thread without going through its own `stop()` — while every status surface kept reporting them as healthy:

- `watcher::live_status()` unconditionally set `status.running = true` whenever a loop was *registered*, regardless of whether its thread had actually died.
- The reminder scheduler had **no liveness surface in `remind_me_server_status` at all** — nothing to check.
- The promotion backlog's `nudge_enabled` field was computed from `promotion::nudge_interval().is_some()` alone: configuration, not "is the loop actually running." A crashed nudge thread and an unconfigured one read identically — both `true` originally isn't right either, both were indistinguishable.

## Fix

Added `scheduler::Liveness`/`LivenessGuard`, a small primitive shared by all three loops (kept in `scheduler.rs` alongside `Stop`, the existing shared shutdown primitive, for the same "written once, reused" reason). A loop's thread holds a `LivenessGuard` for its entire run, bound near the top of its closure; the guard's `Drop` marks the loop dead — during an ordinary return **and** while unwinding from a panic, since `Drop` runs either way. This is a more general answer than `JoinHandle::is_finished()` alone would have been: it doesn't require sharing single-owner `JoinHandle` between a status surface and whatever handle a caller stops the loop with.

- `watcher::live_status()` now reports `liveness.is_alive()` instead of a hardcoded `true`. Everything else about the registration (`scans`, `last_scan_at`, the file counters) still reports even after the thread is gone — only `running` changes meaning.
- `status::ServerStatus` gained a `scheduler: scheduler::SchedulerStatus { running, poll_interval_seconds }` field, always answered (the scheduler has no "configured or not" state to fall back through).
- `promotion.rs` gained `nudge_running()`, backed by the same mechanism. `remind_me_promotion_candidates`'s `nudge_enabled` field now reads that instead of `nudge_interval().is_some()`.

## Verification

```
cargo test --workspace   1791 passed, 0 failed, 134 test binaries
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets   0 warnings
cargo fmt --all --check  clean
```

- Five direct unit tests for `Liveness`/`LivenessGuard` in `scheduler.rs` — including `dropping_the_guard_during_a_panic_still_marks_it_not_alive`, which forces a real unwind through a held guard via `catch_unwind` rather than assuming the `Drop`-runs-on-panic guarantee holds.
- `background_loop_liveness_test.rs` (new) — starts a real scheduler and a real nudge loop against file-backed databases, proving `running: true` while alive and `false` after `stop()`, mirroring `watcher_driver_test.rs`'s existing pattern for the watcher.
- `status_test.rs` gained a test proving a fresh process reports `scheduler.running: false`.

Neither loop has a way to fail mid-run that a test can trigger honestly (no reachable panic path in normal operation), so the integration tests prove the wiring — a started loop reports running, a stopped one doesn't — while the panic-survives-as-dead guarantee itself is proven directly against the primitive.

body:
The controlled fault-injection runner treated any recovery diagnostic as sufficient progress before retrying verification reads. A `StorageConflict` event is emitted before `AbortAndRestore` finishes, so a successful read in that window could be accepted as final and make transient activation state appear to be durable data loss.

Wait for transaction- and grain-correlated recovery completion before verification reads after storage-exception faults. Deactivation faults retain their existing path because replacement activations restore without transaction correlation. Add a deterministic observer regression proving that `StorageConflict` alone does not complete the recovery barrier.

Fixes an issue where package upgrades could install the same configured plugin twice during one update. author: vatsamanoj
body:
Builds out VaultMesh — the standalone, app-agnostic, zero-knowledge decentralized backup cloud — from the P0 central-anchor scaffold (already on `main`) through the full four-phase roadmap. The domain core stays pure and depends only on ports (traits); each phase lands one adapter behind a stable port, so the use-cases never change.

## What's in this PR (5 commits)

**P1 — Reed-Solomon erasure coding + verify-on-restore**
- `adapter-reed-solomon`: any *k* of *n* fixed-size shards reconstruct a blob (default 4-of-6).
- Restore verifies each shard's SHA-256 and treats a corrupted shard as an *erasure*, so RS reconstructs around it within the parity budget.

**P2 — Peer mesh acceleration + anchor fallback**
- `adapter-peer-http`: node-agents replicate/serve shards for each other; reads prefer nearby peers, and the RustFS anchor is always the authoritative fallback — peers offline never blocks a restore.

**P3 — Repair loop, active perimeter, quotas/billing, self-sovereignty**
- `RepairShards`: self-healing reconstruction of missing/corrupt shards on the anchor (+ optional background sweep).
- `adapter-perimeter`: hash-chained, tamper-evident intrusion ledger (`IntrusionSink`) + an escalating allow→tarpit→block responder (`ThreatResponder`), wired as coordinator middleware that records footprints and blocks repeat offenders by fingerprint.
- `UsageReport` + `/v1/usage/{app}` billing; `adapter-rcgen-ca` (self-signed CA, no public CA); `adapter-ddns` (self-hosted naming, the dynamic→static mechanism).

**P4 — Direct QUIC peer-to-peer transport**
- `adapter-quic`: node-agents transfer shards directly over QUIC (`quinn`), end-to-end encrypted on VaultMesh's own self-signed, pinned trust; `DirectNatBroker` punches direct paths with the coordinator relay as fallback. Selectable via `VAULT_TRANSPORT=quic`.

**Docs & demo**
- `docs/WALKTHROUGH.md` + `scripts/demo.sh` (+ `scripts/demo.py`): one command builds, starts a coordinator + two QUIC-meshed node-agents, and runs a narrated end-to-end walkthrough, then the real client-side-encryption roundtrip.
- `README`, `ARCHITECTURE`, `SECURITY`, `ROADMAP` updated per phase.

## Design & quality gates
- SOLID + hexagonal (ports & adapters); every Rust file ≤ 500 lines, enforced in CI.
- `vault-domain` has zero I/O-crate dependencies, enforced by a CI purity check.
- **48 tests pass**; CI runs build, test, `clippy -D warnings`, `rustfmt --check`, the file-size gate, and the domain-purity check.

## Verification
A live run (coordinator + two QUIC-meshed node-agents) exercised the whole flow: 4-of-6 sharding with peer replication over QUIC, byte-identical restore, self-healing repair, peer-served restore after deleting the origin's copy, escalate-to-block on the perimeter with a valid tamper-evident ledger chain, self-signed CA + naming, and a zero-knowledge usage statement. Reproduce with `./scripts/demo.sh`.

Note: `main` was seeded at the P0 scaffold commit so this PR is a clean, fast-forwardable advance; consider making `main` the repository's default branch after merge.

body:
Follow-on to #410 (B2). Two changes that belong together, because writing the
first is what exposed the second.

**Census: `implementations` 0 -> 1 of 74.** Pseudocode unchanged at 43 of 74.

## The entry

`surface-code` gets the graph's first `implementations` entry, written from a
**fetched read of the source** rather than from the record. That is the
distinction the schema draws and the reason this field has sat at 0 while
pseudocode moved: `pseudocode` "can be written from the method's own recorded
contract and step list", an implementation "needs somebody to read a source".

**What the entry does not say is the load-bearing part.** The abstract page names
no processor, no manufacturer and no released artefact, so `data` and `code` are
absent. The device is widely known and is deliberately not written here — naming
it would be recall dressed as a citation, which is exactly the failure #410 spent
twelve rejected listings learning to refuse. Absent means unread, not none.

`results` repeats figures `cost` already carries, deliberately: on the cost card
they are what the method *costs*, here they are what one run *measured*. That is
the distinction the owner's five sub-sections exist to draw. The reading caution
travels with the once-an-hour figure, because it was measured while probing limits
with repetition codes, not observed as the limit of the surface-code memories.

## The section — a live bug this uncovered

**The method page had never drawn `implementations` at all.** Only
`map-card-panel.tsx` did, so this entry would have been reachable through the map
card and invisible to anyone arriving at `/repository/layers/surface-code`:
authored content that ships and is never seen.

This is the same hole #396 closed for `example`, one field along. Worth naming why
it survived — **the census read 0, so nothing rendered because nothing existed,
which is indistinguishable from a section that works.** A renderer for an empty
collection is untested by construction. The general form, now recorded in NEXT.md:
*any field whose count is zero should be assumed undrawn until something proves
otherwise* — check the surface before authoring the first value, not after.

Placed after Cost, where the owner's order puts it (Input, Theory, Output,
Requires, Example, Performance, **Implementations**). The page's existing comment
already follows that order for Example-before-Performance; the page had simply
stopped at the sixth. The empty note states "absent is not zero" in the owner's
terms, because this is the section a reader is most likely to misread as a verdict.

## Verification

- **1008/1008 tests.** `tsc --noEmit` clean, **reading tsc's own exit code** — a
  `| tail` reports the pipe's status and shows a false green in a fresh worktree.
- `pnpm lint` exit 0; `check-math` confirms every `$…$` compiles and both locales
  agree, which covers the LaTeX in the new `results` prose.
- **Read-back with the probe failing first**, on a dev server `lsof`-confirmed
  (parent and listening child) to be serving this worktree:

  | probe | before | after |
  |---|---|---|
  | `Implementations` heading | 0 | 1 |
  | `mj-card-implementations` | 0 | 1 |
  | entry label | 0 | 1 |

  Both locales. `qldpc-code` is the **empty-state control**: it draws the heading
  and the honest note and no list. The paper link and a Results figure both
  render, so the section carries content rather than just a class name.

## Not built, and flagged rather than left implied

Nothing in `apps/web` renders a component in a test (no `lib/*.test.ts` imports a
`.tsx`), so **no guard exists for the next missing section**. The cheap version is
a source-level check that every optional prose field on `LayerMethod` appears in
`repository-layers.tsx`; the real one needs a DOM harness. Recorded in NEXT.md.

## The worklist behind this field, measured

In B2's twelve capabilities alone, **17 methods cite a paper the register marks as
reporting a run**, three of them hardware (`direct-sampling-readout`,
`probabilistic-error-cancellation`, `surface-code` — this one). That is the real
backlog. **It should not be handed to an agent that has not been given the paper:**
#410 measured a ~46% invention rate on transcription where the agent *had* the
record in front of it, and a field requiring a source read, handed to something
without the source, manufactures citations.

## Problem

Three critical issues with timer feature:

1. **Continuous turning bug (CRITICAL):** Game auto-advances turns rapidly, ping-ponging between players
2. **Second player can modify timer:** Joining player shouldn't be able to change timer settings (creator-only)
3. **Timer runs when backgrounded:** Should pause when app backgrounded

## Root Cause Analysis

**Continuous turning:** `autoPassTurn()` flipped turn but never re-stamped `turnStartedAt`. New player's timer started already expired → auto-pass fired immediately again on next tick → turns flipped back-and-forth rapidly.

## Solution

### Step 1: Critical Fix - Re-stamp turnStartedAt on auto-pass

- Now conditionally adds `turnStartedAt` re-stamp when timer is enabled
- Mirrors existing pattern in `placeStone`, `approveUndo`, `rejectUndo`, `resetForRematch`
- **This alone fixes the continuous turning bug**

### Step 2: Background Pause
- File: `GameViewModel.swift`
- Added scene-phase guard in `updateTimerState()` - doesn't tick while backgrounded
- Added timer task cancellation in `appDidEnterBackground()`

### Step 3: Read-only Fetch
- File: `GameRepository.swift` - added protocol method
- File: `FirebaseGameRepository.swift` - added `fetchGame()` for one-shot read

### Step 4: Creator-only Timer Configuration
- File: `PlayView.swift`
- Timer picker hidden when joining existing room
- Shows read-only status: "20s (set by room creator)"
- Only shows editable picker for brand new game creation

## Testing

- [ ] Background app during countdown → timer pauses, resumes correctly
- [ ] Join existing room with timer → see read-only "Xs (set by room creator)"

body:
`project/streaming-infrastructure` was cited in three places as something it does not earn, and my own handoff section about it was wrong in its framing. Both fixed here.

### Base check

```
base            origin/main @ ddea7553
head            origin/evolve/reframe-streaming-reference @ 268033cc
merge-base      ddea7553  == base tip
carries         1 commit(s), 5 file(s)
authors         Peter Kagstrom (1)
top-level       README.md, handbook, project-seed
```

`python project-seed/ci/run_workflows_locally.py` — **all 17 executed steps passed**. `actions/checkout` and `actions/setup-python` are reported `[env ]`, not passed.

### What it was cited as, and what it is

There is **no `quaternionmedia/streaming-infrastructure` repository**. `gh api` returns 404, and `governance-status.yaml` already records exactly that as the project's `repository` value. It is a design branch holding the plan and `ADR-0001` that `main` moved off itself in `dec5c9c`, "Move the math workspace and the streaming project onto their own branches".

| Where | Said | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `README.md` | "the reference instance for a server/container runtime" | there is **no** server/container reference instance — the honest state. Naming that branch invited a forker to copy the setup of a project that was never set up |
| `handbook/forking-a-project.md` | `adr/` "has the most mileage… `streaming-infrastructure` was its first instance" | discounted. It exercised the record format and no other part of a fork; the mileage that counts is the adopting projects |
| `handbook/adoption-audit-queue.md` | an adopting project with "two known content defects" | not an adopting project; there is nothing to audit |

### The correction to my own finding

I wrote that this branch "reports healthy to every check that exists and is genuinely broken". That was facts-true and sentence-wrong — the second interpretive error this session, and the same shape as §8 of the decision-record discipline.

The tip merge is **deliberate and documented**:

> Neutralises the deletion commit on main without discarding anything here, so a future merge from main brings org changes and leaves the payload alone.

`main` deleted the payload; the branch carries it. That is the right intent, and the generated document is honest about the branch besides — `behind_corpus: 40`, `repository: {unknown: 404}`, seed `drift` on both template comparisons.

**The real finding is narrower, and it is about the instrument rather than the decision.** Neutralising a merge declines everything that merge carried, not only the commit you meant to neutralise. Git records the merged commit as incorporated, so no later merge revisits it, and a file returns only if some *later* commit on `main` touches it again:

| Path | Commits touching it after `81d6967` | On the branch today |
|---|---|---|
| `REUSE.toml` | 2 | present — a later commit brought it |
| `LICENSE` | 0 | **absent, permanently** |
| `records/DRAFT-outbound-licensing.md` | 0 | **absent, permanently** |
| `records/DRAFT-version-tags-are-claims.md` | 0 | **absent, permanently** |

Merging `main` into it today conflicts in **22 paths**, so it is not a routine propagation. Nothing here is urgent and nothing is a rule violation — it is written down so whoever does that merge knows those three files will not arrive on their own.

I also corrected a test on the way: my first attempt at this read a working tree mid-conflict (`git merge` exited 1) as though the merge had completed. The table above is from a merge carried to completion.

### One tool fix

`check_pr_base.py` emitted git's raw `rev-parse` error when the head branch was not yet pushed — the normal state when you run it before opening the PR. It now says so.

author: psandana
body:
Fixes #6934.

This revision implements the explicit argument-file option suggested in https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/6934#issuecomment-5256785465.

## Problem

`cargo-fmt` passes every target path for an edition directly to one `rustfmt` process. Windows limits the complete `CreateProcessW` command line to 32,767 UTF-16 code units, so large workspaces fail with OS error 206 before rustfmt starts.

The issue reproducer contains 918 targets and exceeds that limit under a typical absolute checkout path.

## Solution

Rustfmt gains an explicit argument-file option:

```
rustfmt --args-file <path>
rustfmt --args-file=<path>
```

Argument files are UTF-8 with one argument per line. They may be nested up to 16 levels, and `--` terminates option and argument-file expansion globally. Ordinary filenames beginning with `@` retain their existing meaning; no existing positional syntax is reinterpreted.

On Windows, `cargo-fmt` calculates the command-line length using Rust's Windows quoting rules. Only when an invocation would reach 32,767 UTF-16 code units does it write the complete rustfmt argument vector to a temporary file and invoke `rustfmt --args-file <temporary-path>`.

Keeping one rustfmt process per edition preserves existing session, ordering, JSON, and checkstyle behavior. User-provided `--args-file` options are expanded before cargo-fmt creates its transport file, so behavior remains identical below and above the Windows threshold.

## Compatibility

- `@source.rs` remains an ordinary source filename.
- Non-Windows behavior is unchanged.
- Windows commands below the OS limit continue to use direct arguments.
- Argument-file paths and contents must be valid UTF-8, consistent with rustfmt's existing Unicode CLI.
- Embedded newlines are rejected because the format is one argument per line.
- The temporary file remains alive until rustfmt exits.

## Tests

- Separated and `=` syntax, CRLF, blank arguments, missing files, nesting, and global `--` termination.
- An ordinary source filename beginning with `@`.
- Windows command-line quoting and exact length calculation.
- A generated 500-target Windows workspace exceeding the limit.
- User-provided argument files across the cargo-fmt threshold.
- The original #6934 918-target reproducer.

これが入ると **チュートリアルの全コードが CI でコンパイルを通っている**ことが構造的に保証されます。

**生成の仕組み**

body:
## Summary

An external profile put a group send at **387 allocations / 87.7 KiB per message** at 128 members and named `send::encrypt::ensure_sessions_for_devices` as the place to start.

This records what `divan::AllocProfiler` actually measures on this repository's send benches, and — after review — what those numbers do **not** establish. The first revision of this PR claimed they refuted the 387; they do not, and the doc now says so explicitly.

**The result that survives:** a group send that distributes no sender key is **flat in group size** — 22 allocations and 3.58 KB at 10, 50 and 256 members.

## Changes

| File | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `agent_docs/observability.md` | new section — *Per-message allocation on the group stanza build* |

No code changes.

## Cost

`divan::AllocProfiler` as global allocator in `send_receive_benchmark.rs`, 50 samples, pinned to one core. Divan tallies only the benchmarked closure.

**Scope, stated first because it bounds every row:** `run_group_send` calls `prepare_group_stanza` and marshals the node. The client send path around it — group lookup, retry caching, sender-key cache access, `resolve_skdm_targets_memoized`, persistence-adapter construction, the send itself — is outside the measured region.

| stanza build | allocations | bytes |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `bench_dm_send` | 157 | 27.9 KB |
| `bench_group_send_10` (no distribution) | **22** | **3.58 KB** |
| `bench_group_send_50` (no distribution) | **22** | **3.58 KB** |
| `bench_group_send_256` (no distribution) | **22** | **3.58 KB** |
| `bench_group_send_skdm_256` (distributing) | 6,816 | 675.1 KB |

Instruction counts unchanged — nothing executable is touched.

Flat across a 25× range in membership, because the stanza carries one `<enc type="skmsg">` for the whole group and nothing per recipient (pinned separately by `warm_group_send_encoding_scale`, #1281). The DM row is higher because a DM pairwise-encrypts once per recipient device.

## Checked and not changed

Four claims from the first revision were withdrawn after review; each is now documented as a limit rather than a finding:

- **"387 is not reproducible here."** Withdrawn — different scope. 387 came from a full client send; 22 is stanza build plus marshal. The difference is real, unmeasured work.
- **"A warm send never calls `ensure_sessions_for_devices`."** Withdrawn — false for the ordinary linked account. `src/send/mod.rs` states in the `initial_targets` match that own devices are never memoized warm, so **own-only SKDM needs is the warm steady state**: such a send carries a nonempty `distribution_list` on every message. The 22 figure is the zero-own-target case, and the doc now labels it that way.
- **"6,816 = one X3DH plus one pairwise encrypt per device."** Withdrawn — `setup_group_send` calls `establish_session` for every member before forcing distribution, so `ensure_sessions_for_devices` finds each session present and never reaches the prekey-fetch branch. The figure is the SKDM encrypt fan-out plus stanza build (~26.6 allocations per target). **No cold-session cost is measured anywhere in this repository**, and the doc says so rather than implying one.
- **"`resolve_skdm_targets_memoized` minimizes redistribution."** Withdrawn — it memoizes device-set *resolution*. Which devices still need the key is decided by `filter_skdm_targets` against the `SenderKeyDeviceMap` (`device_and_primary_warm`). The doc now points at that map instead.

…objs entre procesos)

Hasta ahora un syncobj solo existía dentro del proceso que lo creó -- sin exportarlo a un fd, no hay forma de que, por ejemplo, un compositor y un cliente Vulkan por separado se pasen fences explícitas entre sí (el caso de uso real detrás de todo el trabajo de syncobjs de esta rama). Este incremento cierra ese hueco reutilizando el MISMO mecanismo que PRIME (dma-buf) ya usa para compartir buffers GEM entre procesos:

- linux-object/src/fs/syncobj_file.rs (nuevo): SyncobjHandle, un objeto FileLike que envuelve un handle u32 de syncobj -- mismo patrón que DmaBuf (dmabuf.rs). Como la tabla de syncobjs es un espacio de handles GLOBAL, no por proceso, "exportar" no mueve ni copia ningún estado: el número de handle ya es válido globalmente, el fd solo lo transporta a través de la tabla de descriptores de otro proceso.
- linux-syscall/src/file/file.rs: nueva sys_drm_syncobj_fd, mismo patrón que sys_drm_prime (ambas necesitan la tabla de fd del proceso, que el io_control a nivel de inodo no tiene). Despacha SYNCOBJ_HANDLE_TO_FD (0xc010_64c1) y FD_TO_HANDLE (0xc010_64c2) -- verificados con la misma fórmula drm_iowr_core ya usada para el resto de las ioctls de syncobj, y cruzados contra el 0xC00C_642E ya hardcodeado de PRIME_HANDLE_TO_FD para confirmar el cálculo. IMPORT_SYNC_FILE (interoperar con un sync_file POSIX real) devuelve EOPNOTSUPP -- Eclipse no tiene esa abstracción. Wireado en sys_ioctl junto al chequeo ya existente de PRIME/CREATE_LEASE.
- kernel-hal/src/drivers.rs: nuevo nouveau_uapi_enabled() (el lado de lectura de set_nouveau_uapi_enabled) -- linux-syscall, a diferencia de linux-object, no depende de zcore-drivers en el target real (solo bajo la feature libos), así que gatea a través de kernel-hal en vez de zcore_drivers:: directo. Encontrado por un error de compilación real al primer intento (E0433 cannot find crate zcore_drivers), corregido antes de comitear.
- drm_scheme.rs: actualizado el comentario que marcaba 0xC1/0xC2 como "fuera de alcance" para reflejar que ahora sí están implementados, solo que en la capa de syscall, no en io_control.

Hueco que queda (documentado en docs/README-nouveau-uapi.md): sin refcounting real -- SYNCOBJ_DESTROY borra la entrada sin importar cuántos fds exportados sigan vivos, a diferencia del DRM real donde un fd exportado mantiene vivo el objeto más allá de un DESTROY sobre el handle que lo exportó. Consistente con que la tabla de syncobjs nunca tuvo refcounting.

author: caspar000
body:
Everything from the MVP through to inline expressions: 37 commits taking Lifeboard from a typed-node
whiteboard to one where any shape can hold data, gather it from the shapes wired to it, and report the
answer inside a sentence you wrote.

## The board

- **Typed-node whiteboard on tldraw** — the MVP, plus a Freeform-style home screen, dotted paper, and
  rename-on-canvas.
- **The note** — live per-line markdown preview, auto-height, tickable checklists in preview, list
  auto-continuation, rebuilt on CodeMirror 6.
- **Light / dark / system theming** across the whole app, with thumbnails that re-export on a theme
  change rather than going stale.
- **Canvas settings** — grid on/off, our grid or tldraw's, and snapping, all independent; rounded
  corners for frames and images on an XS–XL scale.
- **Frames** are transparent outlines with a pickable border colour, and every colourable shape gets
  one swatch that opens a palette above the toolbar.
- **Settings** is a centred column with named sections; tldraw's top-left menu strip is gone, since
  most of it was about a document model this app doesn't have.

## Data on any shape

- **Universal properties** — values live in `shape.meta`, so a photo with a price is the same kind of
  fact as a note with one.
- **Property types**: text, number, financial, date, checkbox, link, select, status, multiSelect,
  rating, progress. `url` folded into `link`; `select` and `multiSelect` became real option menus with
  colours hashed from the option's own text; `status` groups its options into three stages.
- **Money is per shape, not per property** — two cards can carry the same price in different
  currencies, with daily rates fetched, cached and offline-tolerant, and totals that admit when they
  are mixed rather than lying.
- **Background removal** for images — a flood fill, no model — and an auto-trim to the subject after.

## Arrows as relations

- **A drawn arrow is an edge.** Tables and collections can scope to "the arrows pointing at me",
  which is a relation you get by drawing a line rather than by building a junction table.
- **Direction is a sign**: what points in adds, what points away subtracts, so a flow board balances
  without anyone typing negatives.
- **Edge-valued columns** read a property off the *arrow* — "this meal uses 200g of that ingredient"
  belongs to the pairing, and the pairing is a shape that already carries properties.

## Collections, and the end of the table node

- **Any shape can gather.** Switch Collects on for a sticky, note, photo or frame and it reports a
  total, a count, an average, or the list — four controls, no column editor. A table stops being a
  *kind of node* and becomes one way of looking at a set.
- **Results render alongside** what the shape already says, never instead of it.

## `{…}` — a number in the sentence that explains it

- **Inline expressions** in notes, stickies, text shapes, geo labels and arrow labels:
  `Still free: **{sum price either}**`. Substitution is display-only, so the source keeps the
  expression and editing shows it.
- **A helper for writing them** — typing `{` writes its closer and opens a positional menu: the brace
  shows the verbs, a verb shows the properties, a property shows the places to look.
- **One menu, both editors.** The note is CodeMirror and every other shape is tldraw's ProseMirror,
  but the rules and the popup are one shared module rather than two that agree.

## Fixes worth naming

- **Input reached every open tab.** tldraw gates clipboard, shortcuts and document events on one
  `isFocused` flag, and every mounted board set it — so one ⌘V pasted into three boards and one ⌘Z
  undid all of them.
- **A cropped image lost its rounded corners**, because the radius sat on an element that cropping
  resizes to the whole image and slides out of view.
- **Two stale-cache bugs** where a table kept showing an old currency, and a phantom "5 excluded" on a
  total that had excluded nothing.

## Verification

401 unit tests and 74 e2e specs. Every feature here was driven in a real browser before being called
done — several of the bugs above were invisible to a green test suite.

Three e2e tests fail intermittently and are tracked separately, in #2 and #3. Looking into them
properly for those issues corrected what I first reported here, so to be accurate:

- `assets.spec.ts:256` fails **4 of 5 runs in isolation**, and not on its own assertions — it dies in
  the shared `createBoard` helper during setup. Pre-existing. See #2.
- `ui.spec.ts:520` and `ui.spec.ts:374` each pass **5/5 alone** and fail when the whole file runs, so
  the problem is state leaking between tests rather than flakiness. `:520` is pre-existing; **`:374`
  was added on this branch**, so that one is a regression from this work, not a pre-existing issue as
  I first described it. See #3.

One known rough edge: picking a `{…}` suggestion **by mouse** works in the note but not in a sticky —
the pointer-down blurs tldraw's editor and the caret moves out of the expression. Keyboard is solid in
both.

body:
The Langfuse UI is now served at **https://langfuse.toki-tail.com** behind nginx. That turns three things which were survivable on a loopback-only box into things that are not.

## 1. The committed session key made the login decorative

```yaml
NEXTAUTH_SECRET: pawly-langfuse-nextauth-secret-dev   # ← in this repo
```

This signs session JWTs. A published value means anyone who can read the repo can mint a valid session cookie and **skip the password prompt entirely**. Exposing the UI without rotating it would have put an effectively unauthenticated service — holding full system prompts and owner chat messages — on the internet.

It now has **no default**. Compose fails with instructions rather than falling back to something known:

```
required variable LANGFUSE_NEXTAUTH_SECRET is missing a value:
generate with `openssl rand -hex 32` and set in .env
```

The live instance was rotated ahead of exposure; the new value lives in the gitignored `.env`.

## 2. Signup was open, and someone found it

```
admin@pawly.local              2026-04-24 14:02   ← ours
mio-b4f6f1e22fed@example.com   2026-05-16 02:26   ┐
mio-151a1c47cc2e@example.com   2026-05-16 02:27   ├ self-registered, 7 minutes
mio-5ccf05810e51@example.com   2026-05-16 02:33   ┘
```

Random hex addresses, three in seven minutes, all named `mio-ctf` — the shape of a scanner finding an internet-facing signup form. They held **no organization membership**, so they could not read traces or prompts. Deleted, and `AUTH_DISABLE_SIGNUP: "true"` closes the door. Accounts are created by the org owner from the UI.

## 3. Port 3000 was published on every interface

```yaml
ports:
  - "3000:3000"        # before — all interfaces
  - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000"   # after
```

This is the most likely path those accounts took. The production box had been hand-patched to loopback at some point, but the repo still shipped the open version — so any fresh deploy reopened it. nginx is the only public path now.

## Also

`NEXTAUTH_URL` becomes an env var defaulting to localhost, and the override file's copy is removed. That override *restated the default* while being the one thing that could quietly break a deployed instance: it is labelled "not used in production" but lives in the same checkout on the production box, and `docker compose up` reads it unless someone remembers `-f`. A comment is not a guard.

## Deliberately not touched

`SALT` and `ENCRYPTION_KEY` are still dev values (`pawly-langfuse-salt-dev`, all zeros). Rotating `SALT` invalidates the project API keys chat-service authenticates with — it would drop tracing **and** prompt reads the moment it restarts, since prompts now come from Langfuse. That needs a coordinated key reissue into `backend/.env`, not a drive-by edit in this PR.

Same for `LANGFUSE_INIT_USER_PASSWORD: pawly-admin-dev` — it only applies on first boot, so it is inert on the existing instance, but a fresh deploy would create an admin with a known password. Worth fixing in the same pass as SALT.

## Deploy note

`.env` on the box needs two new keys before pulling this:

```
LANGFUSE_NEXTAUTH_SECRET=<the rotated value already live>
LANGFUSE_NEXTAUTH_URL=https://langfuse.toki-tail.com
```

Without them `docker compose` refuses to start the container — by design, but it will stop a deploy.

author: peterblenessy
body:
Refs #459. Stages 2–3 of the triage design, built on the embedding sidecar from #461.

## What lands

**Schema v14: a `census` table** — one cheap embedding score per message, carrying `sender` because the unit of inference is **(conversation, sender)**, not the conversation. Created empty; a scan populates it; no backfill.

**`triage_cells(threshold)`** — the worklist, ranked most-suspicious-first, encoding the heavy-tail argument:

- **Ranks by count of hot messages, not the peak.** One stray high score is noise; density is signal. `triage_ranks_by_density_not_by_the_single_peak` proves a cell with four moderate hits outranks one with a single higher spike — and ranking-by-peak is proven to *fail* that test.
- **Cell = (thread, sender)**, so `one_hot_sender_in_a_crowd_is_ranked_separately`: one abuser among nine ordinary participants is the top row while the thread average stays mild. This is the group-chat case you raised, made a passing test.
- **`trajectory`** is the least-squares score slope per day within a cell, so `a_rising_cell_has_positive_trajectory`: a slow burn that climbs 0.30→0.55 over ten days without ever crossing the hot threshold still surfaces. Advisory context, not part of the sort — one number can't rank two kinds of evidence.

**Incremental**: `census_scored_ids` lets a re-scan embed only new messages.

## Why it's safe to land now

Pure analysis on in-memory data — no model, no scan wiring. Every claim is a unit test. It's the ranking brain the scan loop will call, and it can't regress the shipped scan because nothing calls it yet.

## Next

The scan-loop wiring: run the census over a real backup's messages via `embed()`, then drive focused classification down `triage_cells` with SPRT stopping. That's where the pieces become a pipeline.

`scripts/preflight.sh` clean.

author: znas-io
body:
Closes #3538.

## The defect

Open **Add a cluster** in the VS Code extension, pick Install / Install-guided / Repair, and type one character into any text box. The box loses focus. Every field, every keystroke -- the form can only be filled one click-and-character at a time.

## Root cause

The page posts an `input` message per keystroke, and the host answered it with `render()`:

```ts
this.state.setInput(known, text);
this.render();   // assigns panel.webview.html -- replaces the WHOLE document
```

A full document replacement has no focused element, caret or selection on the other side of it. The repaint *is* the focus loss, once per character. It was there to redraw per-field validation, which on this surface costs a whole-document reload.

## The fix

The keystroke message stays; the render goes. The DOM is discarded on every repaint, so the extension has to be where form state lives -- a screen that stopped recording keystrokes would hand the next render an empty form.

Per-field validation feedback moves to the next action. That is the trade `connectHtml` already documents for the registration form, and for the same reason; every problem is still reported, together, when Start is pressed.

## Scope

Collect screen only. The registration form was never affected -- its inputs carry `data-connect-field`, which `sendField` does not match, so its values are gathered at click time by `connectFields()`. That gather-on-action shape is also `automationPanel`'s, and the collect screen was the sole outlier from it.

## Cover

`StubWebviewPanel` gains a `renders` counter -- assigning `webview.html` is the observable form of "the document being typed into is gone", and it is the only host-side evidence available in a lane with no DOM. Two cases: three keystrokes cause zero repaints (fails on `main` with "three keystrokes repainted the page"), and what was typed is still on screen when a repaint does come.

`npm test`: 979 pass, 0 fail. `npm run compile` clean.

No wire contract change; extension-local.

## 1. Reverse Pec Deck — a duplicate, not a rename

I couldn't rename it as asked, because **"Rear Delt Machine" already existed** — the Rear Delt Fly family's machine variant. Renaming onto that name would have produced two identically-named exercises.

Looking closer, they were the same thing entered twice:

| | Reverse Pec Deck | Rear Delt Machine |
|---|---|---|
| source record | `Reverse_Machine_Flyes` | `Reverse_Machine_Flyes` |
| equipment | machine | machine |
| primary | Rear Delts 5/5 | Rear Delts 5/5 |
| secondaries | Mid/Lower Traps, Rotator Cuff | Mid Traps, Rhomboids |

Same free-db record, same machine in a real gym, split across the Face Pull and Rear Delt Fly families.

So the duplicate is **removed** rather than renamed. The Face Pull family loses its machine slot, and `Reverse Pec Deck` / `Reverse Fly Machine` / `Rear Delt Fly Machine` become aliases of Rear Delt Machine. Searching any of them lands on the one record, and sessions already logged as "Reverse Pec Deck" still resolve to the right muscles.

**215 exercises**, one fewer, no name added.

## 2. Renaming a template only did half its job

This is the "OTHER" bug. A template carries a `name` (what you see in the Plan tab) and a `focus` (what gets stamped onto every session started from it). Rename only touched the name — so a template created as "Other" and renamed afterwards kept starting sessions titled **Other**, which looks exactly like the rename not having worked.

Rename now carries into `focus` too, **but only when the two agreed**. A focus deliberately set to something different is a separate choice and is left alone.

Sessions already logged keep the focus they were given — those are editable one at a time via Edit on the session.

## 3. Finished exercises fold away

Ticking the last set collapses the exercise. That's the moment you're done with it, and a finished card otherwise pushes the next exercise below the fold.

Unticking any set **reopens** it — you only untick to fix something, and fixing it inside a collapsed card is impossible.

## Verification

Chromium at an iPhone viewport:

| check | result |

Given that of the three plugins requested this week one does not exist and one is broken, I checked this one before wiring it in: the package is real at 3.5.0, its dependencies are `css-tree`, `css-select` and `htmlparser2`, and the detectors run offline with no browser and no API key. **The first run found 11 anti-patterns, and 10 are the same thing:** `border-left: 2px solid <accent>`, which it calls the single most recognisable tell of AI-generated interface. The decisions that were previously only in a conversation.

**Accent is `#087cff`** because it is the original declaration and the most frequent literal; the cyan currently winning is an appended theme nobody deleted.

**Nav height is `70px`**, chosen deliberately as *the value already winning*, so collapsing three declarations into one changes nothing visible and any later change to the number becomes a decision rather than a side effect of deleting a block. Same rule for the other eleven duplicated properties.

The prohibitions are written as **named rules rather than a list of ten lines to fix**, because the point is that they stop being written.

## Wiring, and one decision worth reviewing

Impeccable installed its own `.claude/settings.local.json`. I merged its hooks into the committed `.claude/settings.json` and deleted the local file, because a "local" file that has to be committed to work is a trap for exactly the cloud-session reason that put all our hooks in the repo.

- The detectors read CSS and HTML, **not TSX**, so `app/components` contributes nothing to the count today. Real component coverage needs a URL scan against a running app.
- eslint now ignores `.claude/skills`. Vendoring 3.4MB of third-party detector code produced **267 lint errors** in code that is not ours to lint.

Refs #242 (foundation; the full LZ round-trip is a follow-on).

## What changed

- New Anchor workspace under `solana/` with program `bosphor_adapter`:
  - `initialize(authority)` -> `Config` PDA.
  - `submit_intent(blobId, size, encodingType, storageEpochs, deadline)`: derives the keccak intentId via the shared `bosphor-commitment-codec` crate (sender = 32-byte Solana pubkey, per-sender nonce PDA), stores an `IntentState` PDA (`[b"intent", intentId]`) with the committed blob id + terms, emits `IntentSubmitted`. The keccak value is the canonical id; the PDA only holds state.
  - `mark_executed(intentId, returnedBlobId, endEpoch)` (the `_lzReceive` equivalent): authority-gated, requires `!executed` and `returnedBlobId == committedBlobId` (`BlobIdMismatch`), marks executed and records the end epoch.

## Why

Milestone 3, issue #242. The Rust codec landed in #253; this adds the on-chain adapter logic on top of it, now that the Solana toolchain is available.

With `solana`/`anchor` on PATH, from `solana/`:
- `anchor build` -> compiles to SBF (`target/deploy/bosphor_adapter.so`).
- `cargo test` -> codec parity (matches the frozen vectors), adapter intentId parity, and litesvm instruction-level tests (submit + mark_executed happy path, BlobIdMismatch, wrong-authority) all pass offline (no validator needed).

Out of scope here (needs the LayerZero Solana programs + a HITL deploy):

Adds a What's New button beside the donate button that shakes every three seconds until the notes are read, and a dialog that slides up full screen on mobile and fades in at 3/5 by 3/4 on desktop. It also gets its own settings section, with a button to open it and a toggle to keep it off the home screen. The notes are `src/whats-new.md`, rendered by a small Markdown renderer in `core/`; that output goes into innerHTML, so text is escaped and every URL goes through `safeUrl()`, since none of it is this project's own text.

CI overwrites that file with the body of the GitHub release before building. A master build takes the latest published release instead, because Pages deploys from master and would otherwise serve the development placeholder to everyone; a pull request keeps the placeholder, which is what it is there to show. A release with no description now fails the release workflow, since the body is what the page shows.

What gets tracked as read is the notes themselves, stamped by CI as `<!-- release: v0.1.2 -->` or digested when nothing stamped them, rather than the app version. Pages deploys from master, so the PWA usually ships an earlier release's notes than the version around them, and keying on the version would mark the next release's notes read before they existed, on every synced machine at once.

Two things worth a look while reviewing. The dialog pushes a history entry as it opens so Android's back gesture closes it rather than leaving the PWA, and StatusWidget's bottom placement moves from `right-40` to `right-56` to clear a third corner button.

author: copilot
body:
OCR passport scanning was failing to match passengers due to naive string containment logic and no tolerance for OCR errors, accents, or hyphenated names. Search was also limited to `nom` only, missing `prenom` matches entirely.

## Changes

**New helpers**
- `normaliserTexte()` — strips accents, normalizes hyphens/apostrophes to spaces, uppercases
- `levenshtein()` + `tokensSimilaires()` — fuzzy token comparison with tolerance scaled by token length (0/1/2 errors for ≤3/≤6/>6 chars)

**`trouverNomsOCR()` rewrite**
- Anchors on a `DD/MM/YYYY` date pattern; only analyses text *before* the date to cut noise
- Regex now includes `'` and `-` in valid name characters (`DUPONT-MARTIN`, `D'ARCY`)
- Minimum length lowered to 2 characters
- Logs raw OCR text and detected tokens

**`trouverPassagersOCR()` rewrite**
- Searches across both `nom` and `prenom` tokens with OR semantics
- Matching goes through `normaliserTexte()` + `tokensSimilaires()` instead of raw `includes()`
- Logs each match attempt and outcome for easier debugging

```js
// Before: brittle, nom-only, no tolerance
if (p.nom.toUpperCase().includes(nomOCR) ||
    nomOCR.includes(p.nom.toUpperCase().substring(0, 3)))

// After: normalized, fuzzy, nom+prenom
const tousTokens = [...tokensNom, ...tokensPrenom];
const trouve = tousTokens.some(t => tokensSimilaires(tokenOCR, t));
```


`openExternal` is optional and the anchor cancels its own click either way, so no capture — and no unwired host — can navigate the webview. `renderImage` is asked about every image and returns `null` to accept a plain one; GitLab knows nothing about the package.

`apps/desktop/src/components/markdown-loader.tsx` is the container (registered in `CONTAINERS` as *"the Tauri link opener, GitLab source rewriting and the authenticated upload query; its view is markdown, catalogued in @nod/ui"*). It keeps `openExternal`, `stripImageAttributeLists`, and `AuthenticatedUpload` with its `useQuery` + `api.getUploadBlob`, and still exports `Markdown` — the six call sites changed only their import path. The name follows `release-history-loader` / `image-diff-loader`; `coverage.test.ts` requires it not to share a basename with the catalogued component.

react-markdown, remark-gfm, remark-breaks, rehype-raw and rehype-sanitize moved from `apps/desktop` to `packages/ui` dependencies; nothing else in the desktop used them (knip agrees).

### The two `.md` CSS blocks

The global `.md` family (prose + the `.md-suggestion*` card, ~200 lines) is the component's look, so it moved verbatim into `packages/ui/src/markdown/markdown.css`, which `markdown.tsx` imports. What stayed in `quiet.css` are the *host overrides* — rules that name an app surface, not the prose:

- `.dir-quiet .qf-ask-a .md` — an AI answer is aside-weight text in the review pane.
- `.qrh-notes .md` — the release timeline wants smaller, quieter notes than the component's default.
- `.dir-quiet .qf-drawer-body .md { overflow-wrap: anywhere }` — **deleted**, because the component now wraps prose that way everywhere (see below), which is what the drawer was compensating for locally.

Both survivors are now gathered under one "markdown bridges" banner where the family used to live, in ascending specificity order — split across the file they tripped `noDescendingSpecificity`, which the old base `.md` rule had been masking. Comment markers balance: `79 /* · 79 */`.

## Why

`markdown` is the keystone: `comment-item`, `comment-thread` and `review-diff-pane` all render it, and none of them could move while it imported `@tauri-apps/plugin-opener`, `lib/api.ts` and TanStack Query. This unblocks all three.

It also cashes in #280 — inline code renders in `--syn-keyword` from `@nod/tokens` instead of falling back to flat body colour, so the gallery finally shows the real thing.

## Sanitisation

`rehypeRaw` + `[rehypeSanitize, sanitizeSchema]` moved intact, schema (defaults widened by `<details>`/`<summary>`) beside the component. Four fixtures are the standing proof, each carrying its `provenance`:

- `sanitize-script` — `<script>alert(1)</script>`, a `src=` script, and `<svg onload>`: capture is "Before." / "After." with nothing between.
- `sanitize-img-onerror` — `onerror`/`onload`/`onclick` on sources guaranteed to 404, so the error event certainly fires and certainly does nothing.
- `sanitize-javascript-href` — `javascript:` (raw HTML and markdown-authored) plus a `data:text/html` href: the links render, the hrefs do not.
- `raw-html` — the other half: `<b>`, `<i>`, `<kbd>`, `<details>`/`<summary>` survive; `<style>`, `<iframe>`, `<form>` are dropped.

`markdown.test.tsx` asserts the same four things at DOM level (no `script` node, no `on*` attribute, no `javascript:`/`data:` href, `details`/`summary` kept and `iframe` gone) — the sanitiser being load-bearing is exactly the thing that shouldn't rest on a screenshot alone.

## Real bugs the fixtures exposed

1. **Duplicate suggestion lines warned and shared identity.** `SuggestionCard` keyed rows by their own text, so a `` ```suggestion `` with two identical lines (a bare `}`, a blank line — routine) logged *"Encountered two children with the same key"* twice and left React free to duplicate or omit rows. Keyed positionally now; `suggestion-repeated-lines` is the fixture and `markdown.test.tsx` asserts four rows and zero console errors.
2. **Prose had no wrap rule outside the review drawer.** Only `.dir-quiet .qf-drawer-body .md` set `overflow-wrap: anywhere`, so the same body in the inbox or the right panel let a 2,000-character unbreakable token set the block's min-content width. Moved onto `.md` itself (plus `min-width: 0`); `overflow` captures at 280px and 420px pin it.
3. **Wrapping anywhere then wrecked tables.** With cells free to break mid-word the auto layout collapsed columns and rendered `5.62.0` over two lines. Cells opt back out (`overflow-wrap: normal`) and the table scrolls instead (`display: block; width: max-content; max-width: 100%; overflow-x: auto`) — GitHub's arrangement, and better than what the drawer had.
4. **`max-width: 100%` without `height: auto` squashed scaled images.** Any image carrying intrinsic `width`/`height` — which is exactly what `AuthenticatedUpload` passes through — came out of aspect once clamped to the column. Visible in `image-slot`, fixed with `height: auto`.

Worth recording, not a bug: the sanitiser's `src` allowlist is http(s) and relative only, so a pasted `data:` image renders as nothing. The `image` fixture documents it, and it is why hosts resolve their own uploads through `renderImage` rather than inlining a data URL in the source.

## Follow-up recommendation (not in this PR)

`ask-note`'s `renderAnswer` and `release-history`/`whats-new`'s `renderNotes` exist only because Markdown could not move. They can now collapse into a single `openExternal?: (url: string) => void` forwarded to an internal `<Markdown>` — simpler for hosts (a scalar callback, not a render prop), and it deletes three near-identical wrappers in the desktop. Two reasons it is not here: without forwarding `openExternal` the links in release notes would silently stop opening, and the switch rebaselines ~70 captures across the three components, which would bury this port's own diff. `ask-note` also wants a measurement first — it re-renders `partial` on every streamed token, and running remark over half-written markdown at that rate is a different cost from rendering a settled answer.

## Test plan

From the repo root, all green: `pnpm install` · `pnpm exec ultracite fix && pnpm exec ultracite check` · `pnpm typecheck` · `pnpm test` · `pnpm knip` · `pnpm --filter @nod/desktop exec vite build`.

Gallery: `GALLERY_SHOTS_PORT=1485 pnpm run shots:update`, then `pnpm run shots` twice, second run clean. 50 new `-darwin.png` baselines (23 fixtures × 2 themes, plus `overflow` and `suggestion-overflow` at 280px); no pre-existing baseline changed, no `-linux.png` generated.

**The desktop Playwright e2e suite was not run** — it is checked separately.

Stack: sits on #280 (`feat/tokens-syntax-palette`); merge that first.

## Résumé

Audit de sécurité complet (RLS, Storage, secrets, messages d'erreur, validation/recalcul serveur, dépendances, tests d'intrusion en direct — voir `SECURITY.md` pour le référentiel). Rapport détaillé : `docs/SECURITY_AUDIT_PHASE16.md`.

### Critique — corrigé et re-testé en direct

`create_project()` avait une faille d'isolation multi-tenant : sa garde d'autorisation (`get_organization_role(...) not in ('owner','admin','manager')`) ne se déclenchait jamais pour un appelant **sans aucune appartenance** à l'organisation ciblée (`NULL not in (...)` = `NULL`, traité comme faux par PL/pgSQL). Confirmé en exploitant réellement la faille contre le projet Supabase réel : un compte a réussi à créer un chantier dans l'organisation d'un autre compte, via un appel direct à l'API (hors UI). Corrigé avec `coalesce(..., '')` ; ré-exploité après correctif → refusé (`Insufficient organization role`).

### Corrections associées

- Ensemencement des 10 étapes par défaut (Phase 9) silencieusement perdu par deux redéclarations de `create_project()` en Phase 15 — réintégré dans le même correctif, re-testé en direct.
- `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` ajouté sur les 18 tables (défense en profondeur, aucun changement de comportement — l'app n'interroge jamais en tant que propriétaire de table).
- `profiles.phone` supprimée : colonne jamais lue/écrite nulle part dans le code, mais lisible par n'importe qui partageant une organisation/un projet (RLS protège la ligne, pas la colonne) via un appel REST direct.

### Vérifié sans problème trouvé

Secrets (historique git complet), policies Storage, hygiène des messages d'erreur, validation Zod + recalcul serveur systématiques, `npm audit` (0 vulnérabilité sur `apps/web` — les 21 alertes du monorepo sont uniquement dans l'outillage de build Expo/RN, jamais exécuté côté utilisateur).

## Vérification

- `tsc --noEmit` propre sur `apps/web`, `apps/mobile`, `packages/business`.
- Suite Vitest business : 63 tests passent.
- 8 tests d'intrusion exécutés en direct contre le projet Supabase réel (voir tableau dans le rapport) — tous refusés après correctif.
